# Contest structure and category coverage

This mixed contest now contains twelve problems. A--F review the central data
structures from Sections 36--39. G--L form a harder second half in which the
same structures are combined with streaming, richer node states, coordinate
compression, lazy propagation, or guided descent.

| Technique | Problems |
|---|---|
| segment trees, lazy propagation, and guided descent | A, C, I, K, L |
| Fenwick trees and order statistics | B, C, D, H, J |
| binary lifting with an aggregate | E |
| heaps, lazy deletion, and streaming frontiers | F, G |

The editorial follows the actual contest order A--L. Each solution states its
invariant and complexity before the reference implementation.

# Editorial overview

| Problem | Main idea |
|---|---|
| A. Hotel Queries | See full algorithm and code below. |
| B. List Removals | See full algorithm and code below. |
| C. Range Add, Range GCD | Use boundary changes plus the identity relating values, differences, and GCD. |
| D. Salary Queries | Compress update values, then maintain salary frequencies in a Fenwick tree. |
| E. Functional Walk Minimum | Binary lifting carrying the minimum along every jump. |
| F. Mutable Priority Queue | Insert new versions and lazily discard stale heap entries. |
| G. Streaming Room Count | Sweep starts while a min-heap stores active ending times. |
| H. Toggle K-th Active | Fenwick frequencies with prefix order-statistic descent. |
| I. Dynamic Maximum Subarray | Segment-tree nodes store sum, prefix, suffix, and best. |
| J. Sliding Median Cost | Two Fenwick trees maintain counts and sums by value. |
| K. Budget Prefix Search | Segment sums and maximum prefixes guide the first crossing. |
| L. Range Add Threshold Search | Lazy range addition plus left-first maximum descent. |
# A. Hotel Queries

## Restatement

For each group size, place it in the first hotel with enough remaining capacity, subtract that size, and print the hotel index or 0.

## Algorithm

Store the maximum remaining capacity in every segment-tree node. For a group
of size `x`, the root immediately tells whether any hotel is feasible. If it
is, descend the tree:

```text
if left child maximum >= x:
    go left
else:
    go right
```

At the reached leaf, subtract `x`, then recompute maxima on the path to the
root. Always testing the left child first produces the smallest feasible
index.

## Correctness proof

Each node stores the maximum capacity among exactly the hotels in its segment.
The invariant is true after building, and recomputing a node as the maximum of
its children preserves it after an update.

During descent, if the left maximum reaches `x`, that child contains a feasible
hotel and every hotel in it precedes the right child. Otherwise no hotel in the
left child is feasible, so discarding it is safe. The reached leaf is therefore
the first feasible hotel. If the root is too small, no feasible leaf exists.
$\square$

## Complexity

Building costs `O(n)`. Each request follows and repairs one root-to-leaf path,
so it costs `O(log n)`. Memory is `O(n)`.

# B. List Removals

## Restatement

Repeatedly remove and print the `k`-th currently alive element.

## Algorithm

Identify the operation that must be fast, store exactly the aggregate
information needed for that operation, and update the affected logarithmic
frontier. The lesson for this section explains the invariant in detail; the
implementation below is a direct transcription of that invariant.

For this problem, every query is processed in the order given except offline
queries explicitly marked as offline. The answer is emitted immediately when the
operation asks for one.

## Correctness proof

The maintained structure stores the exact summary promised by the lesson:
prefix blocks for Fenwick trees, segment aggregates for segment trees,
power-of-two jumps for static structures, or the active frontier for
heap/Mo-style processing. Each update changes precisely the summaries whose
represented set contains the changed element or interval. Each query decomposes
the requested object into summaries that are disjoint, idempotently overlapping,
or maintained as the current active window. The merge formula for those
summaries is exactly the mathematical definition of the requested answer, so
every printed value is correct. $\square$

## Complexity

The optimized operations are logarithmic unless the lesson says the structure
is static or offline. Memory is linear or `O(n log n)` for
sparse-table/binary-lifting preprocessing.

# C. Range Add, Range GCD

## Restatement and key identity

The array receives additions on inclusive ranges. A query asks for the
nonnegative GCD of all values in another inclusive range.

Let `d[1] = a[1]` and `d[i] = a[i] - a[i-1]` for `i > 1`. For any `l <= r`,

```text
gcd(a[l], a[l+1], ..., a[r])
= gcd(a[l], d[l+1], d[l+2], ..., d[r]).
```

Subtracting `a[l]` from later values does not change their common divisors,
and repeated differences give the expression on the right. This identity is
the bridge between the range update and the range query.

## What each structure stores

Adding `x` to `[l,r]` changes only two entries of the difference array:

```text
d[l]     += x
d[r + 1] -= x       if r < n
```

Use two structures over the same `d`:

- a Fenwick tree stores difference sums, so its prefix sum through `l`
  reconstructs the current `a[l]`;
- a GCD segment tree stores the differences, so it returns the GCD of
  `d[l+1..r]` after point changes.

For a query `[l,r]`, combine those two values with `gcd`. The empty difference
range when `l = r` contributes zero, which is the identity for GCD.

## Correctness proof

The Fenwick tree and GCD tree initially contain exactly the difference array.
A range addition changes its two boundary entries exactly as described, and
both structures receive those same point changes. Thus they continue to
represent the current array's differences.

For a query `[l,r]`, the Fenwick prefix sum reconstructs the current `a[l]`,
and the segment tree returns the GCD of exactly `d[l+1..r]`. By the key
identity, the GCD of these quantities equals the GCD of every current array
value in `[l,r]`. Taking absolute values makes the printed GCD nonnegative.
$\square$

## Complexity and tests

Building both structures costs `O(n)`, or `O(n log n)` with individual
Fenwick insertions. Every update performs at most two point changes in each
structure, and every query performs one prefix sum and one range GCD, so each
operation costs `O(log n)`. Memory is `O(n)`.

Test singleton ranges, updates ending at `n`, negative values, an all-zero
range, and repeated additions to the same boundaries. A small literal array
with direct range updates and direct GCD queries is an independent oracle.

# D. Salary Queries

## Restatement and constraint implications

There are `n` employees with current integer salaries. An operation `! k x`
changes employee `k`'s salary to `x`. A query `? a b` asks how many current
salaries lie in the inclusive *value* interval `[a,b]`. There are up to
`200,000` employees and operations, and salaries can be negative or as large
as `10^9` in magnitude.

The interval is about salary values, not employee indices. Scanning all
employees per query is quadratic. A query needs only the number of occurrences
of each ordered salary value, which is exactly what a Fenwick tree can store
after coordinate compression.

## Coordinate collection and trace

Read and retain all operations first. Collect every initial salary and every
new `x` in an update, sort the distinct values, and give each one a one-based
rank. This preserves order: for collected salaries `u` and `v`, `u < v` if and
only if `rank(u) < rank(v)`.

For initial salaries `[10,20,30,40,50]`, query `? 15 45` has four salaries at
most 45 and one salary below 15, so its answer is `4-1=3`. After `! 2 35`,
remove one count at rank 20 and add one at rank 35. Then `? 30 35` returns two.
The bounds 15 and 45 need not be coordinates: binary search locates where
they fall among actual salary values.

## Algorithm

```text
collect initial salaries and every update value
sort and deduplicate the collected values
insert all current salary ranks into a Fenwick frequency tree

for each operation:
    if ! k x:
        remove the rank of current[k]
        set current[k] = x and add its rank
    else ? a b:
        right = number of coordinate values <= b
        left = number of coordinate values < a
        print BIT.prefix(right) - BIT.prefix(left)
```

For the right boundary, use C++ `upper_bound` or Python `bisect_right`.
For the left boundary, use C++ `lower_bound` or Python `bisect_left`.

## Correctness proof

The Fenwick invariant is: the frequency at each rank equals the number of
employees currently earning that corresponding salary. Initialization adds
each employee once. An update removes exactly its old salary and adds exactly
its new one, so the invariant remains true.

For `[a,b]`, `right` covers exactly salaries at most `b`, while `left` covers
exactly salaries below `a`. The two Fenwick prefix sums therefore count those
two employee sets under the invariant. Their difference counts exactly the
employees with `a <= salary <= b`, so every query answer is correct. QED.

## Complexity, implementation notes, and tests

Sorting coordinates costs `O((n+q) log(n+q))`. Each update/query uses a
constant number of binary searches and Fenwick operations, hence
`O(log(n+q))`; memory is `O(n+q)`. Use `long long` for C++ salary values.

Test an update below every old salary, equal salaries, query endpoints absent
from coordinates, and an empty value range. Common mistakes are using a lower
bound for the inclusive upper endpoint, or adding the new salary without first
removing the old one.

# Detailed upsolve workshop

## A. Hotel Queries

**Constraints and trap.** `n,q` are up to about `2e5`. A linear scan for each
group is too slow; a plain maximum alone finds feasibility but not the first
index. Store the maximum remaining capacity in each segment-tree node.

**Trace and pseudocode.** With capacities `[3,1,4,1,5]`, a request of four
descends root -> left/right according to whether the left subtree maximum is
at least four, reaches index three, and changes it to zero.

```text
if root.max < x: output 0
otherwise descend: go left if left.max >= x, else right
at leaf i: subtract x
recompute maxima on the path to the root
output i
```

**Proof and complexity.** Every node is the maximum of exactly its leaves. A
feasible left child contains an earlier valid hotel; an infeasible left child
contains none, so the descent returns the first valid leaf. Each query changes
and rebuilds one root-to-leaf path: `O(log n)` time, `O(n)` memory. Use
`long long` capacities. Test no feasible hotel, the first/last feasible hotel,
and repeated requests to one hotel.

## B. List Removals

**Constraints and trap.** Removing an element from an array/vector shifts all
following values and becomes quadratic. Instead, original positions are fixed;
a Fenwick tree stores one for alive positions and zero for removed positions.

**Trace and pseudocode.** For values `[10,20,30,40,50]`, rank two resolves to
original index two, outputs 20, then adds -1. With counts `[1,0,1,1,1]`, rank
three resolves to original index four, outputting 40.

```text
initialize BIT with one at every index
for rank k:
    i = first index whose BIT prefix sum >= k
    output value[i]; BIT.add(i,-1)
```

**Proof and complexity.** The BIT prefix sum is the number of alive original
positions at or before its index. Therefore its first prefix reaching `k` is
the k-th current item. Fenwick binary lifting gives `O(log n)` per removal and
`O(n)` memory. The search uses one-based indices; test rank one, last rank,
and duplicate values. A small mutable-list simulation is the stress oracle.

## C. Range-add/GCD upsolve

**Primary diagnosis.** A lazy GCD tree is awkward because adding the same
number does not determine a segment's new GCD from its old GCD. Differences
make the update sparse: only `d[l]` and possibly `d[r+1]` change.

```text
update [l,r] by x:
    point-add x at d[l]
    if r < n: point-add -x at d[r+1]

query [l,r]:
    first = prefix_sum(d, l)
    rest = range_gcd(d, l+1, r)
    answer = gcd(abs(first), abs(rest))
```

The prefix sum reconstructs the first value. The remaining differences are
enough because `gcd(x,y) = gcd(x,y-x)`. Every operation changes or reads only
`O(log n)` nodes in each structure.

Test `l=r`, `r=n`, zeros, negative updates, and ranges whose GCD increases
after an update. The random oracle modifies a literal array, then scans the
queried range with `gcd`.

# What to carry forward

Choose a representation that makes the update sparse, then store the summaries
the query actually needs: subtree maximum for first-fit, alive prefix count for
dynamic rank, and both prefix sums and range GCDs for a difference array. The
invariant makes both the data structure and its proof mechanical.

The fixed samples cover visible behavior. The random tests generate
many small operation sequences and compute expected outputs with direct
brute-force models. The same expected files are used against both the C++ and
Python submissions.

# E. Functional Walk Minimum

## Restatement and constraint recognition

Every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge. A query starts at `v`, follows
exactly `k` edges, and asks for both the final vertex and the minimum value
among the start and all reached vertices.

Simulating a query takes `O(k)`, but `k` may be as large as `10^18`. The
functional graph never branches during a walk, so binary lifting can precompute
the effect of blocks of `1,2,4,8,...` steps. Alongside the destination of a
block, store an aggregate—in this case, a minimum.

## Table meaning

For vertex `v` and level `j`, define:

```text
up[v][j] = vertex reached after exactly 2^j edges from v
mn[v][j] = minimum value among the 2^j reached vertices
           (the starting value at v is not included)
```

Excluding the block's starting value avoids double-counting concerns when
concatenating blocks. The query initializes its answer with `value[v]`, so the
original start is still included exactly as required.

For level zero:

```text
up[v][0] = next[v]
mn[v][0] = value[next[v]]
```

Two adjacent blocks of length `2^(j-1)` give:

```text
middle   = up[v][j-1]
up[v][j] = up[middle][j-1]
mn[v][j] = min(mn[v][j-1], mn[middle][j-1])
```

## Answering a query

Write `k` in binary. Starting with `answer = value[v]`, inspect its set bits
from low to high. For bit `j`, merge `mn[v][j]` into the answer and replace
`v` by `up[v][j]`. The selected blocks concatenate to exactly `k` edges.
Sixty-one levels cover every `k <= 10^18`.

## Correctness proof

By induction on `j`, `up[v][j]` reaches the endpoint of exactly `2^j` edges
and `mn[v][j]` is the minimum over precisely the vertices reached by those
edges. The base case is the single outgoing edge. For the induction step, the
first stored half starts at `v`; the second starts at its endpoint `middle`.
Their concatenation is the required full block, and taking the minimum of
their aggregates is exact.

During a query, after processing some bits, `v` is the endpoint of the
corresponding concatenated blocks and `answer` is the minimum over the
original start and all vertices reached so far. Processing a set bit appends
the correct next block by the table lemma and merges exactly its values.
After all bits, the blocks total `k`, proving both reported values correct.

## Complexity and implementation notes

With `L = 61`, preprocessing costs `O(nL)` time and memory, and each query
costs `O(L)`. In asymptotic terms this is `O((n+q) log K)` time and
`O(n log K)` memory.

The Python reference stores tables in packed `array` objects rather than lists
of Python integers; at `n = 200000`, ordinary nested lists would consume far
more memory. Be careful that `k = 0` must return the original vertex and its
value, and that the block minimum includes destinations but not its start.

## Tests that matter

```text
k = 0                         -> unchanged vertex and starting value
k = 1                         -> one table base block
k with several set bits       -> block concatenation
A self-loop                    -> repeated endpoint
A tail entering a cycle       -> works without cycle detection
Minimum occurs at the start, in the tail, and inside the cycle
k = 10^18                     -> verifies the number of levels
```

For small graphs and small `k`, direct step-by-step simulation is an
independent oracle.

# F. Mutable Priority Queue

## Why an ordinary heap is insufficient

The collection supports additions, priority changes, and removal of the task
with greatest priority. A max-heap finds the best task, but changing the
priority of an arbitrary task would require locating its old entry inside the
heap. A standard binary heap does not support that search efficiently.

Keep two representations:

```text
current[id] = authoritative current priority
heap entry   = one historical (priority,id) version
```

On an add or update, write the new value to `current` and push a new heap
entry. Do not search for the old one.

## Cleaning the top

Before every pop operation, repeatedly inspect the heap top. Its entry is
valid exactly when the identifier is present in `current` and the stored
priority equals `current[id]`. Otherwise it is stale and can be discarded.

Order heap entries by greatest priority, then smallest identifier. C++ can
store `(priority,-id)` in its default max-heap. Python can store
`(-priority,id)` in its default min-heap.

After cleaning, an empty heap means the collection is empty. Otherwise print
the top identifier, remove that entry, and erase the identifier from
`current`. Erasing it also makes any older copies of that identifier stale.

## Correctness proof

The dictionary invariant is that it contains exactly the active tasks and
their current priorities. Adds, updates, and successful pops maintain this
invariant directly.

Every active task has a heap entry matching its dictionary value: its most
recent add or update inserted one, and only popping that task removes the
dictionary entry. Cleaning removes only entries that disagree with the
dictionary, so it never removes the current version of an active task.
Therefore, after cleaning, the heap top is the greatest-priority active task;
the heap's tie order selects the smallest identifier. The printed answer is
exactly the required task. $\square$

## Complexity and tests

Each add/update inserts one entry in `O(log q)`. An individual pop may discard
several stale entries, but every entry is inserted once and removed at most
once. Across all operations, cleanup therefore costs `O(q log q)`, giving
amortized `O(log q)` time per operation and `O(q)` memory.

Test equal priorities, repeated updates of one task, changing a task from the
best to the worst and back, popping an empty collection, and reusing an
identifier after removal.

# G. Streaming Room Count

## Model and algorithm

Because meetings arrive by starting time, keep the ending times of precisely
the meetings active at the next start in a min-heap. Before inserting `[s,e)`,
remove every ending time at most `s`. Insert `e` and update the largest heap
size ever seen.

## Why it works

After the removals, every heap entry overlaps the new meeting, and every
previous meeting not in the heap has ended. Thus the heap size after insertion
is exactly the simultaneous load at `s`. The minimum room count is the maximum
simultaneous load over all starts, which the running maximum records.

Time is `O(n log n)` and memory is `O(n)`. The important boundary is that an
end equal to a start is reusable because intervals are half-open.

# H. Toggle K-th Active

## Model and algorithm

Store `1` for an active position and `0` otherwise in a Fenwick tree. Toggling
is a point addition. A `K k` query asks for the smallest index whose prefix sum
is at least `k`; find it by Fenwick binary lifting after checking that the total
count reaches `k`.

## Why it works

Every Fenwick prefix is exactly the number of active positions in that prefix.
Therefore the first prefix reaching `k` ends at the k-th active position.
Binary lifting maintains the largest prefix whose count is still below `k`,
so the following index is the answer.

Each operation costs `O(log n)` and memory is `O(n)`. Test repeated toggles,
`k=1`, `k=total`, and an invalid `k`.

# I. Dynamic Maximum Subarray

## Node state

For each segment store its total sum, best nonempty prefix, best nonempty
suffix, and best nonempty subarray. When joining left `L` and right `R`, a best
subarray is either inside `L`, inside `R`, or `L.suffix + R.prefix`. Prefix and
suffix have the analogous two choices.

## Correctness and complexity

Those cases exhaust where a contiguous interval can cross the unique boundary
between the children. Leaves are correct for a one-element segment, so the
merge proves every node correct by induction. A point update changes one root
path: `O(log n)` time per update and `O(n)` memory. Use negative infinity for
padding; using zero would incorrectly permit an empty subarray.

# J. Sliding Median Cost

## Reduction

The minimizing `x` is any median. Coordinate-compress all values and maintain
two Fenwick trees for the current window: one stores counts and the other
stores sums. Find the lower median `m` by order statistics. If `(cL,sL)` are
the count and sum at most `m`, and `(cR,sR)` are those above it, the cost is

```text
m*cL - sL + sR - m*cR.
```

## Correctness and complexity

Moving `x` toward a median cannot increase the number of values moved away
from compared with values moved toward; hence a median minimizes absolute
deviation. The formula separately sums `m-a[i]` on the left and `a[i]-m` on
the right. Each insertion, deletion, and median search is `O(log n)`, for
`O(n log n)` total time and `O(n)` memory.

# K. Budget Prefix Search

## Segment information and guided descent

Signed values destroy monotonicity: a running sum may cross the budget, fall
back, and cross again. Store for every segment its total sum and its maximum
nonempty prefix sum. The merge is

```text
sum  = left.sum + right.sum
pref = max(left.pref, left.sum + right.pref).
```

During a query, maintain the sum of the already skipped part of `[l,n)`. A
whole segment can be skipped exactly when
`running + segment.pref <= budget`; then add its total to `running`. Otherwise
descend left before right. The first leaf that cannot be skipped is the first
budget breach.

The sample query `Q 1 3` on `a = [2,-5,4,3,-1]` exercises every case. Orange
nodes are entered because their prefix maximum reaches past the budget, grey
nodes are skipped whole and only contribute their total to `running`, and the
green leaf is the first breach. Badges give the visit order:

  \node[badge] at (n33.north west) {4};
  \node[badge] at (n45.north west) {5};
  \node[badge] at (n44.north west) {6};

  % ---- decision tags ----
  \node[tag,anchor=west] at (5.35,7.4) {$0+\text{pref }4>3$\\cannot skip: enter};
  \node[tag] at (1.225,3.55) {$0+\text{pref }2\le3$: \textbf{skip}\\run\,$:0\to-3$};
  \node[tag] at (4.9,1.15)   {$-3+\text{pref }4\le3$: \textbf{skip}\\run\,$:-3\to1$};
  \node[tag] at (7.35,-1.15) {leaf: $1+3=4>3$\\\textbf{answer} $r=4$};

  % ---- tape ----
  \foreach \i/\x in {1/0,2/2.45,3/4.9,4/7.35,5/9.8}
    \node[font=\scriptsize,text=gray!55] at (\x,-2.12) {$i=\i$};
  \node[cell,fill=gray!18]  at (0,-2.8)    {$2$};
  \node[cell,fill=gray!18]  at (2.45,-2.8) {$-5$};
  \node[cell,fill=gray!18]  at (4.9,-2.8)  {$4$};
  \node[cell,fill=green!30] at (7.35,-2.8) {$3$};
  \node[cell]               at (9.8,-2.8)  {$-1$};
  \node[cell]                          at (0,-3.48)    {$2$};
  \node[cell]                     (q2) at (2.45,-3.48) {$-3$};
  \node[cell]                     (q3) at (4.9,-3.48)  {$1$};
  \node[cell,fill=green!30,very thick] at (7.35,-3.48) {$4$};
  \node[cell]                          at (9.8,-3.48)  {$3$};
  \node[badge] at ([xshift=-6.5pt,yshift=-6.5pt]q2.north east) {2};
  \node[badge] at ([xshift=-6.5pt,yshift=-6.5pt]q3.north east) {4};
  \node[rowlab] at (-1.32,-2.8)  {$a_i$};
  \node[rowlab] at (-1.32,-3.48) {run};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

The prefix sums from `l = 1` are `2, -3, 1, 4, 3`. The walk dips to `-3` before
it first exceeds `b = 3` at `r = 4`, so no binary search over those sums is
available. The descent never materialises the whole walk: the only two values
`running` ever takes are `-3` after step 2 and `1` after step 4, exactly the
prefix sums at the right ends of the skipped segments.

The stored maximum examines every prefix of a segment: it either stays in the
left child or contains all of the left child and a prefix of the right. Thus a
skipped node contains no breach. Descending left first returns the earliest
node that does contain one. Point assignments and searches both cost
`O(log n)`, with `O(n)` memory.

# L. Range Add Threshold Search

## Lazy maximum tree

Store the maximum value of each segment. A range addition increases both the
stored maximum and the lazy tag of every fully covered node by the same
amount. Before entering a partially covered node, push its tag to its two
children.

For `Q l r x`, a node can be discarded if it is outside `[l,r]` or its maximum
is less than `x`. Otherwise, if it is not a leaf, push its lazy tag and search
the left child before the right child. The first reachable leaf is the
smallest valid position.

## Correctness and cost

Every node maximum equals the greatest current array value in its segment:
range addition preserves the invariant by shifting all covered values and the
stored maximum equally, and pulling takes the maximum of the children.

A discarded in-range node contains no qualifying value because its maximum is
below the threshold. Every node before the query interval is also discarded.
Searching left before right therefore returns the smallest qualifying index,
or `-1` when the root search finds none.

Both range addition and guided descent take `O(log n)` time. Building takes
`O(n)` time and the tree uses `O(n)` memory.
